title: Gilded Void - Nightmare Logic
author: Old-Entertainment844
selftext:
Gilded Void is a liminal, weird survivors-like that shouldn't make sense, but does. It's free, it's in Beta, and it plays in your browser. (Desktop Only for now, mobile coming soon)

🎮 Play: [https://seladori.itch.io/gilded-void](https://seladori.itch.io/gilded-void)  
🎬 Trailer: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0z02mmVRkw8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0z02mmVRkw8)

**The budget:**

* **Hardware:** an old Inspiron with no GPU and 8 GB of RAM.
* **Money:** about £100 in total, all of it £20-a-month subscriptions.
* **Time:** about ten weeks from first playable to Beta.
* **Team:** me.

**The tools:**

* **Code:** GPT 5.5, Sol 5.6, Astra 6.0 and Claude Opus 5.5, used as agents.
* **Sprites and artwork:** GPT models.
* **Music:** ElevenLabs.
* **Direction, design, taste, and 150+ hours of playtesting:** me.

**What it is:** You're a damaged Centroid in the Shattered Diagram. Every weapon you take becomes a ring around you, and the order you take them in shapes your build, so you grow from one fragile ring into a rotating mandala. There are 8 stages, each with a Hard Mode, 15 bosses, 21 weapon rings, 18 playable Centroids, Boss Rush, Rival Diagrams and a 43-node skill tree. The aesthetic comes from my childhood nightmares.

**The potato was the design document.** "It has to run on my machine" was a founding rule, not an afterthought. There's no engine, just a canvas in a browser tab, and every effect, enemy and particle had to earn its place in a frame budget set by a computer with no graphics card. If it stutters on mine, it doesn't ship. The upside is that if your machine is newer than a toaster, it'll run.

**How the work splits:** The AI does the grunt work. I supply the ideas and the thousands of micro-decisions that add up to something resembling a game. I set the direction, play it constantly, and approve or reject every change by eye and feel. The agents implement, test and document.

**What I learned:**

* **Never assume, check everything.** Agents will tell you something is fixed and be wrong. Play it, look at it, measure it.
* **Back up regularly.** Especially when the computer is a potato.
* **Agents are brilliant at systems and terrible at "feel".** Measuring every sprite's real silhouette so hits land on the art took an afternoon. Getting a black screen to fade out the same way it faded in took most of a day of me saying "make it shorter."
* **Document and plan everything.** Every change went into a running plan: what was built, why, and whether I'd approved it. That's what kept months of work coherent across sessions and across models.
* **Your best ideas come from playing, not reading code.** "Double movement speed if you're touching a wall" became wall-grinding, and it's one of my favourite things in the game.

It's free, and always will be. There's an optional donation, and every penny goes towards a computer with an actual GPU. I'd love feedback, especially on balance and on how it runs on modest machines. I'm reading every comment on the itch page.

comments.author: ShadowFalcon1
comments.body: I'm just curious, you mentioned backing up but surely a project this big should have a github repository. Then just have the AI remember to commit and push changes every so often.

replies.author: Old-Entertainment844
replies.body: Sorry for the confusion. I do use github as my means of backing up.
